newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS-Ukraine plans more output, wage debts remain.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ukraine plans more output, wage debts remain.

text.p: Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko on Tuesday announced a new government programme aimed at helping domestic industrial producers boost flagging output, but offered little hope to Ukrainian workers unpaid for months.

"Maintaining and protecting domestic production, and the national production sector as a whole holds the central place in our government plan," Lazarenko told parliament, which must approve the three-year plan.
But he also said Ukraine cannot immediately solve its $1.7 billion wage payment crisis.

"We can handle this problem step by step, by paying out 200 million hryvnia ($117 million) a month," Lazarenko told the chamber. "But I can't promise that the government can solve this problem immediately."
Lazarenko said 40 projects were under preparation to support and attract investment for large exporters like aircraft, bus, and combine makers, plus 17 new laws to boost the sector.
The government will also implement tax reform to ease pressure on producers, and retain value-added tax on cigarettes, alcohol and expensive consumer items, he added.

"The current tax system could lead to a national catastrophe," Lazarenko said. President Leonid Kuchma has promised to reform high taxes next year. The taxes have been largely blamed for the huge black economy.
Ukraine owes back wages and benefits to teachers, doctors, civil servants, miners, students and pensioners.

Lazarenko said only 13 million of Ukraine's 52 million people are working -- official statistics say there are only three million unemployed -- and that Ukraine is supporting 15 million pensioners and paying benefits to 18 million people.
"This type of situation is unique in the world," Lazarenko said.
Economy Minister Vasyl Hureyev said that, based on the new programme, industrial output would grow 1.7 percent next year. Ukraine's September industrial production fell nine percent from a year ago.
"The chief task is to stop a drop in production which has been going on for five years, and to get production going again," Hureyev told Reuters.
The government plan will also extend to the agricultural sector, with protection of inefficient large state-run operations which are the country's main food producers.

Figures based on the 1997 draft budget, to be presented to parliament this week, foresee the first economic growth since the fall of Communism, with gross domestic product (GDP) seen growing 1.7 percent after a plunge of 11.8 percent last year.

Roman Shpek, head of the National Agency for Reconstruction and Development, said Ukraine will also increase production by doubling foreign investments by the end of 1997, from the $1.1 billion received since independence five years ago.
"The government wants to reduce the number of foreign credits, and instead receive and increase investment," he said.
Ukraine expects to receive $2.5 billion in foreign credits in 1997, mainly from bodies like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, he added.
He said work with the IMF and Bank would continue with an eye to increasing foreign investment.

"Foreign investors observe how Ukraine gets along with funding bodies," said Shpek. He said investors would be impressed with Ukraine's recent taming of inflation and a 1997 deficit projected at two percent of GDP.
